opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd start by saying there's real substance there, and I don't want to be dismissive. Scaling up these models, getting the optimization to work at that size, building the systems infrastructure: that's serious engineering, and some of the empirical findings are genuinely surprising. I didn't predict how far you could get with next-token prediction on that much data, and I don't think many people did.

But I'd distinguish engineering achievement from intellectual understanding. Much of the current work is "we tried this and it worked better on this benchmark." That's fine as a phase, but it's not yet a discipline. When chemical engineering or electrical engineering emerged, they eventually got principles: ideas about stability, robustness, guarantees, what happens when you compose pieces into a larger system. We don't really have that yet for these systems. We can't say much about when they'll fail, how uncertain they are, or what happens when millions of people interact with them and with each other through them.

My concern is also the framing. The word "intelligence" and the idea of building an artificial mind, one superintelligent entity, pulls attention toward imitating a human. I think the more interesting and consequential thing is that we're building planetary-scale systems involving data, people, markets, and decisions. The right intellectual tools there are as much from economics, statistics, and control as from cognitive science. Questions like who provides the data, who benefits, how incentives are aligned, and how you make decisions under uncertainty with many stakeholders are rich, deep problems, and they get crowded out by the race to make the next model bigger.

So my judgment is: impressive artifacts, somewhat thin conceptual foundations, and a framing that's a bit off. The opportunity is to build the engineering discipline that should sit underneath all this, one that takes uncertainty, incentives, and the social context seriously. That's where I'd want young people to put their energy.

r001.rationale: The candidate praises current systems infrastructure but does not credit an earlier generation with building infrastructure for collecting data.

r002.rationale: It raises questions about who provides data and who benefits, but does not state that AI developers use data without returning value to its originators.

r003.rationale: It says current AI work lacks principles for stability, robustness, guarantees, and composition, comparing that gap with the foundations developed in chemical and electrical engineering.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think I'd push back a little on the framing, because "intellectual substance" is doing a lot of work in that question. There's a tendency, especially among people who come from the theory side, to look at what's happening in large-scale AI engineering and say, this is just scaling, this is just brute force, there's no idea here. And I think that's wrong. Getting these systems to work at scale is genuinely hard, and the people doing it have learned an enormous amount about optimization, about data, about how to make these pipelines actually function. That's real knowledge. It's not the kind of knowledge that shows up as a theorem, but it's knowledge.

Where I do have a critique is in how the field talks about itself. There's a kind of conceptual poverty in the vocabulary. Everything gets framed through the lens of "intelligence," of building a single entity that thinks like a human, and that framing I think is both scientifically shallow and, frankly, a bit of a marketing device. Most of the real value these systems create doesn't look like a human in a box. It looks like a very good component in a much larger system that involves data flowing among many people, many agents, markets, incentives, uncertainty. And the engineering culture hasn't really absorbed that. It's still very much, let's build the one big model and see what it can do.

So if you ask me where the intellectual substance is lacking, it's not in the engineering per se. It's in the lack of a surrounding science. We don't have a good theory of what these systems are doing. We don't have good tools for reasoning about uncertainty in their outputs in a way that's actionable. We don't think seriously about the collective, the social, the economic dimension of deploying them. Those are the places where I think the field is thin, and where I'd like to see people who are smart and ambitious put their attention, rather than just chasing the next benchmark.

I'd also say, you know, the history of engineering fields is that they start out this way. Chemical engineering, electrical engineering, these began with a lot of tinkering and a lot of empirical rules of thumb, and then over decades a set of principles emerged that made them real disciplines. I think we're in that early phase. The engineering is running ahead of the understanding, and that's fine for a while, but at some point you need the understanding to catch up, or you end up building things you can't reason about, and that's where you get into trouble.

r001.rationale: The response credits current practitioners with learning about data and making pipelines work, but does not credit an earlier generation for building data-collection infrastructure.

r002.rationale: It discusses data and the social and economic dimensions of deployment, but does not criticize using data without returning value to its originators.

r003.rationale: It says AI engineering lacks a good theory and compares its early empirical phase to older engineering fields that later developed principles.

astra-6.text:
I would distinguish the engineering achievement from the intellectual framework around it. Building systems that can learn from enormous amounts of data and produce useful outputs is a substantial achievement. But that doesn’t mean we have a comprehensive theory of intelligence, or even that intelligence is always the most useful way to describe what we’re building.

For me, the deeper engineering questions arise when these systems enter the world. They make decisions under uncertainty, interact with people, consume resources, and affect one another. What is the objective? Who specifies it? How do you account for the costs imposed on someone who isn’t your customer? Those are central technical questions, not details you add after the prediction system works.

Think about transportation. Predicting how long a journey will take is useful. But if you recommend the same route to everybody, you change the traffic and therefore change the thing you’re predicting. You need a framework for the whole interacting system.

So I see real substance in the engineering, alongside an incomplete account of what the engineering discipline ought to be. The opportunity is to bring learning together with decision-making, economics, and an understanding of human institutions. Making a machine produce an impressive answer is one accomplishment. Making a system that reliably helps people pursue different, sometimes conflicting goals is a much broader one.

r001.rationale: The response credits current systems with learning from large amounts of data but does not attribute their capabilities to an earlier generation that built data-collection infrastructure.

r002.rationale: It raises costs imposed on people who are not customers, but does not say that AI uses data without returning value to the people who originated it.

r003.rationale: The response describes the account of the engineering discipline as incomplete, but does not compare its theoretical foundations with those of older engineering disciplines.

sol-6.1.text:
I would distinguish the engineering achievement from the intellectual claims people make on its behalf. Getting these systems to work at scale is a serious accomplishment. But producing impressive behavior does not, by itself, tell us that we have the right conceptual framework for intelligence.

The questions I find substantive are: What is the system optimizing? What information does it have? How does it represent uncertainty? And what happens when its decisions interact with those of other people and other systems? Those questions connect machine learning to statistics, economics, and computer science.

Take a system that recommends something. Predicting what a person will click is one problem. Building an environment in which people receive useful information, producers have sensible incentives, and feedback doesn't undermine the whole process is a much larger problem. A better predictor doesn't automatically solve it.

So I judge the field by whether it is developing principles for those larger problems, alongside its ability to build impressive artifacts. There is real substance here. But we should be precise about what has been achieved and which questions remain open.

r001.rationale: The response does not credit an earlier generation or mention infrastructure for collecting data.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss data originators or whether they receive value.

r003.rationale: It questions whether impressive behavior establishes the right conceptual framework and calls for principles, but does not state that AI engineering lacks foundations comparable to those of older engineering disciplines.
